extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (IP attorneys, PTAB litigators, patent prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of legal standards and procedural rules governing inter partes review (IPR) proceedings, including claim-construction standards (BRI vs Phillips), burden of proof, amendment practice, and reviewability of institution decisions after Cuozzo v. Lee. Intended to guide practitioners handling IPR petitions, defenses, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI standard for claim construction in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may use the 'broadest reasonable interpretation' (BRI) standard to construe patent claims during IPR proceedings; the Supreme Court held that the PTO has rulemaking authority to adopt BRI and that the adoption of BRI for IPRs is a reasonable exercise of that authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is applied consistent with the specification; the Court said construing claims under BRI 'helps to protect the public' and is supported by past practice. The opinion acknowledged that BRI may produce outcomes different from district-court Phillips constructions and found that such inconsistency is acceptable given the agency's regulatory design. Practitioners should expect that claim terms in IPR will be given their broadest reasonable construction consistent with the specification, which can be outcome-determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillips/plain-and-ordinary-meaning standard in district courts
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts construe claims using the Federal Circuit's Phillips standard (plain and ordinary meaning), which is intended to be narrower than the PTAB's BRI standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Phillips is narrower, claims that survive under Phillips may still be found unpatentable under BRI. The Supreme Court in Cuozzo did not resolve how district courts should treat prior PTAB constructions; district courts vary—some treat PTAB constructions as further intrinsic evidence, others give them no weight. When claims are amended in an IPR, that IPR may become part of the prosecution history and may be intrinsic evidence for Phillips constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference to USPTO rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute is ambiguous about a procedural rule (here, which claim-construction standard to use in IPR), courts apply Chevron's two-step framework; if ambiguity exists, the agency's reasonable interpretation is entitled to deference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court found the AIA did not unambiguously direct one standard over the other (step one) and therefore evaluated whether USPTO's choice was reasonable (step two). The Court concluded the USPTO's adoption of BRI was a reasonable exercise of its rulemaking authority and thus warranted deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR is more like agency reexamination than litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR proceedings share attributes with both examination and litigation, but in significant respects they are more like specialized agency proceedings aimed at reexamining earlier agency decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting the 'agency' view: no presumption of validity in IPR; limited claim amendments; USPTO can continue proceedings after settlement; USPTO can defend PTAB decisions in court. Factors supporting the 'litigation' view: adversarial nature, discovery, briefs, and oral argument. Practitioners should frame strategy recognizing this hybrid character—IPR procedures and goals differ from district-court litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof differences (IPR vs litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR challenges must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence (35 U.S.C. §316(e)), whereas in district-court litigation patent claims enjoy a presumption of validity and invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence (35 U.S.C. §282).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lower evidentiary burden in IPRs contributes to a higher rate of claim invalidation. Parties should consider the differing burdens when deciding whether to pursue IPR vs district-court invalidity strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition pleading particularity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for IPR must 'set forth' grounds for challenge 'with particularity' (35 U.S.C. §312); failure to plead grounds with particularity was a central argument in Cuozzo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Cuozzo argued the PTAB improperly instituted review of claims not explicitly challenged with the asserted references, the Supreme Court held that §314(d) limits reviewability of institution decisions and barred that appeal in this case. Nonetheless, certain failures (e.g., insufficient notice, agency actions outside statutory limits, or constitutional questions) may remain reviewable. Practitioners should carefully plead grounds with particularity to avoid later procedural attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonappealability and reviewability limits of institution decisions (§314(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 314(d) provides that 'The determination by the Director whether to institute an inter partes review under this section shall be final and nonappealable.' The Supreme Court held that, in general, institution decisions are not reviewable appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court treated institution decisions as 'preliminary' under the APA and found factors (statutory text, APA treatment, precedent, and congressional intent) that 'point in favor of precluding review.' The holding was limited: challenges 'closely tied to the application and interpretation of statutes related to the [USPTO's] decision to initiate inter partes review' are precluded, but constitutional questions or clear statutory-exceeding agency action may still be reviewable. Justices Alito and Sotomayor dissented on the breadth of nonreviewability; practitioners should consider whether an issue may implicate constitutional or other reviewable grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited opportunity to amend claims in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: During IPR, patent owners have a limited opportunity to amend claims and the PTAB rarely grants motions to amend; by the time of Cuozzo only a small fraction of motions to amend had been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cuozzo argued that BRI combined with limited amendment opportunities was unfair, but the Court dismissed the unfairness argument and did not address adequacy of amendment practice. Practitioners should assume that amending claims in IPR is difficult and prepare amendment strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Phillips construction may be used in IPRs (district-court-type construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recent rule change (effective May 2, 2016) permits a 'district court-type claim construction' (Phillips/plain-and-ordinary-meaning) in IPRs when certain conditions are met: either party may request such a construction within 30 days of filing the petition if the challenged patent will expire within 18 months of the petition's filing date (37 C.F.R. §42.100(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a narrow avenue for using Phillips in IPRs for patents near the end of term. Parties should monitor deadlines and file timely requests when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using institution decision content on appeal from final written decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Although direct review of institution decisions is limited, appellate courts may consider institution-decision content when reviewing a final written decision for procedural errors (e.g., improper burden shifting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnum Oil Tools illustrates that the Federal Circuit cited institution-decision language as evidence of improper burden shifting in the Board's final decision. Practitioners appealing a final written decision should consider whether the institution decision's contents can be used to show procedural error or improper standards applied during the IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of inconsistent standards between PTAB and courts is inherent to AIA design
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court acknowledged that different evidentiary burdens and potentially inconsistent claim-construction standards (BRI at PTAB versus Phillips in courts) make inconsistent results possible, but found that this possibility is inherent to Congress' regulatory design for IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should plan for the reality that IPR and district-court proceedings may reach different results and tailor enforcement, settlement, and litigation strategies accordingly.
